notes.b: A wedding takes a day, but a marriage lasts years. Pre-marriage courses give engaged couples a structured chance to examine what married life involves before they commit.
points: A pre-marriage course is run before the wedding and helps a couple understand what married life involves and prepares them for it.
Courses explain the expectations and realities of marriage, so couples test their assumptions about married life before the wedding rather than discovering a mismatch afterwards.
Accord, an Irish marriage and relationship support organisation founded by the Catholic Church, provides pre-marriage courses for couples in centres around Ireland. It is not a State body.
Churches and other religious bodies also offer preparation for their own members, and some may require it before a religious wedding. The couple should check the requirements of their own religion.
notes.tip: Pre-marriage courses are not marriage counselling. Courses prepare couples before the wedding, while counselling helps couples who are already in difficulty.

notes.b: Courses cover a range of practical and personal topics, so couples can discuss them before the wedding.
points: Topics include communication, conflict resolution (managing disagreements), relationships, family planning, child-rearing and parenting, financial responsibility and budgeting, and the legal requirements of marriage.
Practical topics include buying or renting a home and managing the household budget as a married couple, so money and housing plans are agreed before they cause disputes.
Couples discuss roles and expectations, such as who will do which household tasks and what each partner expects from the marriage.
Couples examine their own personal qualities that help a marriage, such as honesty, openness, tolerance and commitment, and discuss issues that could harm the marriage.
Courses prompt couples to discuss problems such as addiction (alcohol abuse, drugs and gambling), so they can recognise the warning signs and know where to seek help early.
notes.tip: When asked what a course covers, do not just list topics. Pair each topic with the problem it prevents, for example finance, so the couple can plan a budget and avoid money disputes.

notes.b: Exams ask how courses help, not only what they cover. Each benefit below follows from the topics: the course gives couples knowledge, skills and a safe place to talk.
points: They explain the expectations and realities of marriage, so couples test their assumptions before committing.
They encourage openness and honest communication between partners, so difficult subjects are raised before the wedding instead of after it.
They give couples a forum to discuss shared expectations about roles, money, housing and having children, and to find out whether they agree.
They give practical advice on money, housing, parenting and family planning, so the couple can plan ahead.
They build the skills needed to resolve conflict before it damages the relationship, which reduces the risk of later breakdown, and they show couples where help is available.
Meeting other engaged couples gives support and shows couples that others have the same questions.
notes.tip: If asked to discuss how courses help, give each benefit with its reason. Examiners reward answers that say what a topic is and how it helps, not a bare list of topics.

notes.h: Other facilities and services for couples preparing for marriage
notes.b: Pre-marriage courses are not the only help available. The State, schools, religious bodies and advice services all play a part in preparing people for marriage.
points: The registrar of the area (the civil registration service) receives the written notice of intention to marry at least three months before the wedding, and the couple supply the required documents.
The registrar also inspects proposed venues, so the ceremony location is approved, and registers the marriage.
Religious bodies may offer preparation for couples before a religious wedding, and the couple should check the requirements of their own religion.

Schools prepare young people for marriage: Home Economics classes examine the roles and responsibilities of partners in marriage and the laws relating to marriage, and SPHE classes discuss relationships and marriage.

Information and advice services help with specific questions: Citizens Information, solicitors for legal questions such as property and wills, financial advice services such as MABS for budgeting, and the family's own support.
notes.tip: When asked about the role of the school, name both subjects and what each does: Home Economics studies the roles and responsibilities of partners and the laws on marriage, and SPHE discusses relationships.

keyTerms.definition: A course that prepares couples for the expectations, realities and responsibilities of marriage before the wedding.
The process by which partners identify disagreements and reach a solution both can accept.
Decisions a couple makes about whether and when to have children, and how many to have.
A relationship between two people, based on how they communicate, cooperate and treat each other.
The beliefs each partner holds about the roles, responsibilities and outcomes of married life.
The registrar for the area where the wedding takes place, who receives the notice of intention to marry and registers the marriage.

factCards.term: Four topics covered in a pre-marriage course
factCards.definition: Communication, conflict resolution, family planning and finance, all of which affect how the marriage functions.
It encourages openness, lets couples discuss expectations, gives advice on housing, money, parenting and family planning, and helps them recognise problems such as addiction.

factCards.term: Role of schools in marriage preparation
factCards.definition: Home Economics and SPHE classes examine the roles and responsibilities of partners and the laws relating to marriage.

factCards.term: Irish provider of marriage preparation courses
factCards.definition: Accord, an Irish marriage and relationship support organisation.

questions.prompt: Name two facilities or services available to couples preparing for marriage in Ireland, and describe what each provides.
questions.model: Any two of the following, each described: pre-marriage courses, such as those offered by Accord, which explain the expectations and realities of marriage and give advice on finance, family planning and communication; the registrar of the area, who receives the written notice of intention to marry at least three months before the wedding, approves venues and registers the marriage; religious preparation offered by churches or other religious bodies before a religious wedding; school subjects such as Home Economics and SPHE, which examine the roles and responsibilities of partners and the laws relating to marriage.

questions.prompt: Explain how a pre-marriage course can help a couple prepare for married life, identifying the topics it covers and the problems it helps them to anticipate.
questions.model: Topics: the course covers communication, conflict resolution, relationships, family planning, child-rearing, finance, the legal requirements of marriage and buying a home. How it helps: it explains the expectations and realities of marriage, so the couple test their assumptions; it encourages openness and gives them a forum to discuss shared expectations about roles, money and children; it builds the skills to resolve conflict before it damages the relationship. Problems anticipated: couples examine their personal qualities, such as honesty, and discuss issues that could harm the marriage, including addiction and alcohol abuse, and learn to recognise them and seek help early.
